newsitem.title: FRANCE: Grudging France acknowledges Zaire takeover.
newsitem.headline: Grudging France acknowledges Zaire takeover.

text.p: France grudgingly acknowledged on Saturday the takeover of Zaire by rebel leader Laurent Kabila, seen as a setback for the conservative government at the height of a parliamentary election campaign.

The Foreign Ministry, voicing regret that the conflict was ended through arms rather than talks, said it held Kabila responsible for the security of foreigners and would closely monitor his first moves before deciding on relations with his government.
A ministry spokesman said foreign nationals were not in danger and there was no plan at the moment to evacuate them.

A ministry statement said the new leaders must rapidly work with all of Zaire's political forces for national reconciliation and democratic elections and they should let a United Nations mission investigate reports that the rebels massacred refugees in the east of the country.
"We will closely monitor the new authorities' moves. We will define our relations with them according to their acts," the ministry said.
France had kept an embarrassed silence since Zaire's veteran ruler Mobutu Sese Seko fled to his home village of Gbadolite on Friday.
A ministry spokesman said he had no indications whether Mobutu might seek exile in France, where he has often stayed during the past few months.
Analysts said the government would not be keen to give him shelter, at least until after the May 25-June 1 polls for fear that his presence should become an election issue.
Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin was prompt to bring up the rout of France's ally into the election campaign.

"What is happening in Zaire certainly seals in a way the failure of France's African policy. The government was wrong to put Mobutu back in the saddle after we had tried to sideline him," he told reporters on the campaign trail.
Like other major powers, France had ostracised Mobutu for his autocratic rule and record on corruption and human rights.
A French Socialist cabinet minister once described him as "a walking safe in a leopard-skin hat" and he was at one point barred from entering France and staying at his Riviera mansion.

But he regained Paris' favour three years ago by allowing French troops to use bases in Zaire during their 1994 operation to stop revenge massacres of Hutus in Rwanda following the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

France's past support for Rwanda's ousted Hutu-led government weighed heavily on its policy which seemed hopelessly overtaken by events as Kabila's Rwanda-backed, Tutsi-led rebels took over a swathe of eastern Zaire last October.

A French bid to send a multinational force to eastern Zaire to protect Rwandan Hutu refugees was approved by the United Nations despite U.S. reluctance, only to be dropped as large numbers of refugees returned home and the rebels feared the force would be used to keep Mobutu in power.
French officials, saying Paris was working with Washington to ensure a peaceful transition in Zaire, sought to play down France's diplomatic isolation through the crisis.

But France was clearly sidelined, and the changeover in one of the world's biggest French-speaking countries marked a sharp loss of influence on a continent which it has long regarded as its backyard.

Ironically, the French daily Le Monde commented, France has few economic interests in the mineral-rich former Belgian colony where the biggest investors are Belgium, the United States and South Africa.
"The mistake of sticking by Mobutu over the past few years was all the worse," it said.
